text:
The apple lodged in Gregor's back is left in place because nobody is willing to take it out, so it stays as a permanent visible sign of his injury.

The passage opens Part III, which is the start of the section that follows the wounding of Gregor by his father's thrown apple p. 47. Gregor is still alive, but his injury is serious and the apple is embedded in his flesh. The phrase "No-one dared" signals that his family and the household fear the task of removing it, and it implies that the wound is now part of Gregor's condition.

Here the apple becomes a lasting symbol: it marks the violence Gregor has suffered and the way the family treats him as a burden rather than as a son and brother.

text:
Gregor's sister, Grete, is saying the family must find a way to remove Gregor, whom they now see as a monster. The line comes near the end of Part III p. 61 and is repeated and developed a few lines later p. 62.

The line is spoken by Grete to her father, and it is the turning point of the story. Her "it" refers to the creature Gregor has become, and "get rid of" means removing him from the flat, whether by abandoning him or worse. Her words also show her weariness: she says the family has done "all that's humanly possible" and can no longer endure the strain p. 61.

Here the phrase marks the moment the family's patience ends. Gregor has spent weeks hoping to be accepted, and his failed attempt to reach his sister's music shows how far the family has turned against him. The sentence makes clear that the family's response to his suffering has moved from pity to a decision to be rid of him.

The objection: the family's decision to get rid of Gregor is presented as a settled moral conclusion, yet the text gives it no real counterweight.

Grete's line on page 62 frames the wish to be rid of him as a necessary response to suffering: "We've done all that's humanly possible to look after it and be patient, I don't think anyone could accuse us of doing anything wrong." A critic could argue this self-justification is unreliable, since the family has already been shown to resent Gregor's support, and their earlier fantasies of the conservatory and of a better flat were built on his labour. The text on page 62 also records that Gregor "had lain still" and "was weak from hunger," meaning the family's account of his threat is filtered through their own fear. The author's best reply, drawn from the passage, is that the narrative lets the reader see Gregor's humanity and the family's failure, so the verdict is meant to implicate them rather than vindicate them.

text:
Gregor's father threw it. On page 46, after the chase around the room, he fills his pockets with fruit from the bowl on the sideboard and bombards Gregor, throwing one apple after another without taking careful aim. Most glance off, but one hits squarely and lodges in Gregor's back p. 46.

It matters for a few reasons the document itself points to. First, it is the wound that cripples him: he loses much of his mobility, probably permanently, and is reduced to the condition of an ancient invalid p. 47. Second, it stays in his flesh because no one dares remove it, so it becomes a visible reminder of the injury. That reminder is what makes even his father recall that Gregor is a family member who cannot be treated as an enemy, and that the family has a duty to be patient p. 47. Third, it keeps hurting and later rots. Near the end Gregor can hardly feel the decayed apple in his back, as his pain fades before he dies p. 65.

The text does not say outright that the apple kills him. That reading is an interpretation, though the narrative clearly ties his decline to the injury.

text:
The document gives Grete's own stated reasons, and they are mostly about exhaustion and survival. She says the family has done everything humanly possible to look after Gregor and be patient, and that no one could accuse them of wrongdoing p. 62. She argues that the family cannot keep working as hard as it does and then come home "to be tortured like this," and she fears it will be the death of both parents p. 62.

The immediate trigger is the scene with the lodgers. Gregor's appearance in the living room drives them to give notice, and that costs the family the rent it had come to depend on p. 61. Grete's speech comes straight after.

She also says she can no longer call him her brother, and later insists the family must give up believing the creature is Gregor, since the real Gregor would have left of his own free will p. 63. That is her rationalization for treating him as an animal.

The narrator suggests another layer. Gregor notices that her care had already turned into indifference, with food pushed in with her foot p. 51. Beyond that, the document does not explain her feelings further; the strain of work, shame, and revulsion are the readings it supports.

Part III

Part III follows the Samsa household in the weeks after Gregor's injury, as the family's patience and money wear thin. It brings the story to its close, so it settles what Gregor's transformation finally means for the people around him.

Where we are

Gregor lies injured in his room, an apple lodged in his back, more than a month after his father's attack. p. 47
The family is poor and exhausted: the maid is gone, jewellery is sold, and everyone works, though the flat is too big for their means. p. 50
A room in the flat has been let to three bearded gentlemen, and clutter and rubbish are being pushed into Gregor's room. p. 54

People

Gregor — The transformed son, once the family's provider, now weak, mostly confined to his room, and watching them through the door.
Grete — His sister, who works in a shop, studies shorthand and French, and plays the violin; she once cared for Gregor closely.
Mr. Samsa — The father, now working as a bank employee, who wears his uniform even at home and dozes in his chair.
Mrs. Samsa — The mother, asthmatic, who sews underwear for a fashion shop and wants to look after Gregor.
The charwoman — A strong elderly widow who does the heavy work and is not afraid of Gregor.
The three gentlemen — Fussy, tidy lodgers who take a room in the flat and expect order.

Threads to watch

The family's patience with Gregor is stretched by money worries and fatigue, and the care for him is changing. p. 51
Grete's claim over cleaning Gregor's room causes a bitter family row and shows how her feelings toward him have shifted. p. 52
Gregor, still drawn to music and to his old plan for Grete, wonders whether he is an animal at all. p. 58
The lodgers' presence puts pressure on the household to keep Gregor hidden. p. 55
